claim: High myopia is a significant risk factor for several blinding eye diseases including glaucoma, retinal detachment, and macular degeneration.
source: High myopia is a significant risk factor for several blinding eye diseases including glaucoma, retinal detachment, and macular degeneration, and therefore represents a leading cause of blindness worldwide (Buch et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buch et al., 2001

claim: High myopia represents a leading cause of blindness worldwide.
source: High myopia is a significant risk factor for several blinding eye diseases including glaucoma, retinal detachment, and macular degeneration, and therefore represents a leading cause of blindness worldwide (Buch et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Buch et al., 2001

claim: The prevalence of myopia is continuing to increase and is predicted to affect nearly half of the global population by 2050.
source: The prevalence of myopia is continuing to increase and is predicted to affect nearly half of the global population by 2050 (Holden et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Holden et al., 2016

claim: Normal eye growth (emmetropization) is controlled by visual input.
source: Although clinical and experimental studies indicate that normal eye growth (emmetropization) is controlled by visual input (Wallman and Winawer, 2004), the molecular mechanisms underlying myopia development in humans is not understood.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wallman and Winawer, 2004

claim: The molecular mechanisms underlying myopia development in humans is not understood.
source: Although clinical and experimental studies indicate that normal eye growth (emmetropization) is controlled by visual input (Wallman and Winawer, 2004), the molecular mechanisms underlying myopia development in humans is not understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field

claim: Deprivation of form vision results in accelerated ocular growth and the development of myopia within a matter of days in many vertebrate species, including fish, chicks, mice, tree shrews, guinea pigs, and primates.
source: Deprivation of form vision, through the use of visual 'occluders' or 'goggles' results in accelerated ocular growth and the development of myopia within a matter of days in many vertebrate species, including fish, chicks, mice, tree shrews, guinea pigs, and primates (Howlett and McFadden, 2006; Shen et al., 2005; Schaeffel et al., 2004; Tejedor and de la Villa, 2003; Troilo and Judge, 1993; Wallman et al., 1978; Sherman et al., 1977).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Upon removal of the occluder, the elongated eye experiences myopic defocus, which results in a rapid deceleration in ocular elongation and eventual return to emmetropia (recovery).
source: Upon removal of the occluder, the elongated eye now experiences myopic defocus, which results in a rapid deceleration in ocular elongation and eventual return to emmetropia (recovery) (Wallman and Adams, 1987).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wallman and Adams, 1987

claim: The eye has been shown to compensate for imposed defocus in many vertebrates, including fish, chicks, mice, mammals, and primates.
source: Postnatal ocular growth can also be manipulated through the application of positive or negative lenses, as the eye has been shown to compensate for the imposed defocus in many vertebrates, including fish, chicks, mice, mammals, and primates (Tkatchenko et al., 2010; Shen and Sivak, 2007; Norton et al., 2006; Graham and Judge, 1999; Hung et al., 1995; Schaeffel et al., 1988).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: Application of positive lenses results in images forming in front of the retina (myopic defocus).
source: Application of positive lenses results in images forming in front of the retina (myopic defocus).
evidence: This is established knowledge about optical principles

claim: Imposed myopic defocus causes slowing of the rate of ocular elongation and thickening of the choroid.
source: This imposed myopic defocus causes slowing of the rate of ocular elongation and thickening of the choroid, which effectively pushes the retina toward the image plane, thereby minimizing the imposed refractive error (Wallman et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wallman et al., 1995

claim: Application of negative lenses moves the image plane behind the retina (hyperopic defocus) and results in an increased rate of axial elongation and thinning of the choroid.
source: Conversely, application of negative lenses moves the image plane behind the retina (hyperopic defocus) and results in an increased rate of axial elongation and thinning of the choroid to pull the retina back toward the image plane.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field

claim: Visually induced changes in ocular growth are the result of a locally driven 'retina-to-choroid-to-scleral molecular signaling cascade'.
source: It is well established that visually induced changes in ocular growth are the result of a locally driven 'retina-to-choroid-to-scleral molecular signaling cascade' that is initiated by a visual stimulus, followed by biochemical and structural changes in the retina and choroid, ultimately resulting in altered extracellular matrix (ECM) remodeling of the scleral shell (Troilo and Smith, 2019; Tkatchenko et al., 2006; Fischer and Reh, 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The choroid undergoes changes in thickness, permeability, and blood flow during periods of visually guided eye growth.
source: The choroid, a highly vascularized layer located immediately adjacent to the sclera, has been shown to undergo changes in thickness, permeability, and blood flow during periods of visually guided eye growth (Rada and Palmer, 2007; Fitzgerald et al., 2002; Pendrak et al., 2000; Wallman et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claim: The choroid is suspected to synthesize and/or release scleral growth regulators to control the rate of ocular elongation in response to visual stimuli.
source: Moreover, due to its proximity to the sclera, the choroid is suspected to synthesize and/or release scleral growth regulators to control the rate of ocular elongation in response to visual stimuli (Rada and Palmer, 2007; Marzani and Wallman, 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rada and Palmer, 2007 and Marzani and Wallman, 1997

claim: All-trans-retinoic acid is one potential choroidally derived scleral growth regulator, whose choroidal concentrations are modulated by the activity of retinaldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (RALDH2).
source: All-trans-retinoic acid is one potential choroidally derived scleral growth regulator, whose choroidal concentrations are modulated by the activity of retinaldehyde dehydrogenase 2 (RALDH2) (Rada et al., 2012; Mertz and Wallman, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Rada et al., 2012 and Mertz and Wallman, 2000

claim: IL-6 is expressed in numerous cells throughout the choroid and RPE as punctate cytoplasmic deposits.
source: Immunohistochemical staining for IL‐6 indicated that IL-6 is expressed in numerous cells throughout the choroid and RPE as punctate cytoplasmic deposits, some of which appeared to colocalize with nuclei of RPE and choroidal cells (Figure 1A and B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical data shown in figures

claim: IL-6-containing cells included the RPE, choroidal endothelial cells, and choroidal stromal cells.
source: IL-6-containing cells included the RPE, choroidal endothelial cells (arrowheads; blood vessels are labeled with asterisks), and choroidal stromal cells.
evidence: Supported by immunohistochemical observations

source: Immunolabeling was abolished after preabsorption of this antibody with a tenfold molar excess of chicken IL-6 demonstrating that the immunohistochemical detection procedure was specific (Figure 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental control shown in Figure 1C

claim: Administration of the non-specific inhibitor NOS inhibitor, Na-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME), or the nNOS inhibitor Nw -propyl-L-arginine, blocks recovery from form deprivation myopia (FDM), or compensation to +10 D lens-induced defocus due to inhibition of choroidal thickening and dis-inhibition of scleral proteoglycan synthesis.

Administration of the non-specific inhibitor NOS inhibitor, Na-nitro-L-arginine methyl ester (L-NAME), or the nNOS inhibitor Nw -propyl-L-arginine, blocks recovery from form deprivation myopia (FDM), or compensation to +10 D lens-induced defocus due to inhibition of choroidal thickening and dis-inhibition of scleral proteoglycan synthesis (Nickla et al., 2009; Nickla and Wildsoet, 2004).

claim: Intravitreal treatment with L-NAME significantly attenuated the recovery-induced increase in choroidal IL-6 gene expression, indicating that nitric oxide either directly or indirectly regulates choroidal IL-6 gene expression.
source: We found that intravitreal treatment with L-NAME significantly attenuated the recovery-induced increase in choroidal IL-6 gene expression, indicating that nitric oxide either directly or indirectly regulates choroidal IL-6 gene expression.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Treatment of isolated choroids with the NO donor, PAPA-NONOate stimulated IL-6 gene, and protein expression, confirming that choroidal IL-6 is upregulated by NO.
source: Treatment of isolated choroids with the NO donor, PAPA-NONOate stimulated IL-6 gene, and protein expression, confirming that choroidal IL-6 is upregulated by NO.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 7A and B

claim: NO has been reported to stimulate IL-6 production in skeletal myocytes, human blood mononuclear cells, and kidney epithelial cells by activating ERK1/2 and p38 MAPK-signaling pathways.
source: NO has been reported to stimulate IL-6 production in skeletal myocytes (Makris et al., 2010), human blood mononuclear cells (Siednienko et al., 2011), and kidney epithelial cells (Demirel et al., 2012) by activating ERK1/2 and p38 MAPK-signaling pathways.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: p38 MAPK signaling was crucial for the PAPA-NONOate-mediated activation of IL-6 in chick choroids as incubation with the p38 MAPK inhibitor, SB203580, abolished PAPA-NONOate-stimulation of IL-6 gene expression.
source: We also found that p38 MAPK signaling was crucial for the PAPA-NONOate-mediated activation of IL-6 in chick choroids as incubation with the p38 MAPK inhibitor, SB203580, abolished PAPA-NONOate-stimulation of IL-6 gene expression.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR data shown in Figure 7C

claim: Daytime levels of retinal dopamine were shown to be reduced in form deprived chick and monkey eyes.
source: Daytime levels of retinal dopamine were shown to be reduced in form deprived chick (Stone et al., 1989) and monkey eyes (Iuvone et al., 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stone et al., 1989 and Iuvone et al., 1989

claim: Intravitreal injections of apomorphine or dopamine prevented the development of deprivation myopia.
source: Furthermore, intravitreal injections of apomorphine (Stone et al., 1989; Iuvone et al., 1991) or dopamine (Gao et al., 2006) prevented the development of deprivation myopia.
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Nickla et al., 2013 demonstrated that the dopamine agonist, quinpirole, prevented the development of myopia via a nitric oxide-dependent mechanism, indicating that dopamine acts upstream of NO in the signal cascade mediating ocular growth inhibition.
source: Interestingly, Nickla et al., 2013 demonstrated that the dopamine agonist, quinpirole, prevented the development of myopia via a nitric oxide-dependent mechanism, indicating that dopamine acts upstream of NO in the signal cascade mediating ocular growth inhibition.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nickla et al., 2013

claim: NO and nNOS (NOS1) have been detected in virtually all types of retinal neurons, in the RPE, and in several cell types in the chick choroid.
source: NO and nNOS (NOS1) have been detected in virtually all types of retinal neurons, in the RPE, and in several cell types in the chick choroid (Fischer and Stell, 1999; Eldred, 2000).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fischer and Stell, 1999 and Eldred, 2000

claim: Treatment of isolated choroids with the NOS substrate, L-arginine, in the presence of 50 mM KCl can upregulate choroidal IL-6 transcription.
source: Our finding suggests that treatment of isolated choroids with the NOS substrate, L-arginine, in the presence of 50 mM KCl can similarly upregulate choroidal IL-6 transcription that suggests the endogenous sources of nitric oxide within the choroid have the potential to regulate IL-6 mRNA and protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR data shown in Figure 8

claim: Atropine has been shown to prevent experimentally induced myopia in chicks and inhibits myopia development in some children when applied topically.
source: Atropine has been shown to prevent experimentally induced myopia in chicks and inhibits myopia development in some children when applied topically (Chia et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chia et al., 2012

claim: A single intravitreal injection of atropine to chicks undergoing form deprivation-induced myopia stimulated choroidal IL-6 gene expression.
source: We found that a single intravitreal injection of atropine to chicks undergoing form deprivation-induced myopia stimulated choroidal IL-6 gene expression.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR data shown in Figure 9A

claim: Incubation of isolated choroids with 0.1% atropine stimulated choroidal IL-6 gene and protein expression, suggesting that atropine acts directly on the choroid to stimulate IL-6 synthesis.
source: Moreover, incubation of isolated choroids with 0.1% atropine also stimulated choroidal IL-6 gene and protein expression, suggesting that atropine acts directly on the choroid to stimulate IL-6 synthesis.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR and ELISA data shown in Figure 9B and C

claim: Choroidal IL-6 is a likely player in the retina-to-sclera signaling cascade underpinning visually guided ocular growth.
source: The results of the present study indicate that choroidal IL-6 is a likely player in the retina-to-sclera signaling cascade underpinning visually guided ocular growth (Figure 10).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cumulative data presented in the study

claim: IL-6 transcription has been shown to be regulated by a number of factors, including steroid hormones, glucocorticoids, TNF-α, interferon-γ, Il-1b, epidermal growth factor, and amphiregulin.
source: IL-6 transcription has been shown to be regulated by a number of factors, including steroid hormones, glucocorticoids, TNF-α, interferon-γ, Il-1b, epidermal growth factor, and amphiregulin (Luo and Zheng, 2016; Bersinger et al., 2011; Lisi et al., 2010 Mahtouk et al., 2005), and some of these mediators have been implicated in myopia development (Dong et al., 2019; Dong et al., 2020; Ding et al., 2018; Gong et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies

claim: Choroidal IL-6 is associated with a slowing of eye growth, as it is upregulated in recovering eyes (when eyes are decelerating their rate of elongation) and in myopic eyes treated with atropine, an agent known to inhibit vitreous chamber elongation and myopia.
source: In the context of ocular growth control, it appears that choroidal IL-6 is associated with a slowing of eye growth, as it is upregulated in recovering eyes (when eyes are decelerating their rate of elongation) and in myopic eyes treated with atropine, an agent known to inhibit vitreous chamber elongation and myopia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the data presented in the study

claim: IL-6 mRNA is downregulated in recovering eyes treated with L-NAME, a compound known to inhibit recovery and increase scleral proteoglycan synthesis and ocular elongation.
source: Moreover, IL-6 mRNA is downregulated in recovering eyes treated with L-NAME, a compound known to inhibit recovery and increase scleral proteoglycan synthesis and ocular elongation.
evidence: Supported by TaqMan real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6A

claim: Treatment of isolated sclera with IL-6 had no effect on scleral proteoglycan synthesis.
source: Treatment of isolated sclera with IL-6 had no effect on scleral proteoglycan synthesis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), indicating that additional downstream mediators, most likely derived from the choroid, are responsible for regulating the scleral changes associated with recovery.
evidence: Supported by scleral proteoglycan synthesis assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: IL-6 has a major role in the pathology of uveitis, glaucoma, retinal vein occlusion, macula edema, and diabetic retinopathy.
source: On the other hand, studies have shown that IL-6 has a major role in the pathology of uveitis, glaucoma, retinal vein occlusion, macula edema, and diabetic retinopathy (Zahir-Jouzdani et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zahir-Jouzdani et al., 2017

claim: IL-6 induces ocular inflammatory responses often leading to the breakdown of the blood ocular barrier, angiogenesis, increased vascular permeability, and choroidal neovascularization.
source: IL-6 induces ocular inflammatory responses often leading to the breakdown of the blood ocular barrier, angiogenesis, increased vascular permeability, and choroidal neovascularization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about IL-6 function

claim: Myopic defocus in humans, as a result of uncorrected myopia, may cause elevated choroidal IL-6 which could predispose individuals to serious ocular complications.
source: Based on the results of the present study, it is possible that myopic defocus in humans, as a result of uncorrected myopia, may cause elevated choroidal IL-6 which could predispose individuals to one or more of the above serious ocular complications.
evidence: This is speculation based on the study findings

claim: Monocular form-deprivation of chicks resulted in a large negative shift in refractive error.
source: Monocular form-deprivation of chicks in this study resulted in a large negative shift in refractive error. Data are represented as mean ± standard errors. *p=0.0313 Wilcoxon matched-pairs signed-rank test for n=6 birds.
evidence: Supported by photorefraction data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claim: Application of –15 D lenses results in a hyperopic shift in the refraction of normal chick eyes, relative to untreated (no lens) eyes.
source: Application of –15 D lenses results in a hyperopic shift in the refraction of normal chick eyes, relative to untreated (no lens) eyes, whereas application of +15 D lenses results in a myopic shift in refraction, compared to untreated eyes. ***p<0.0001, ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for n=2 chicks in each group (five measurements/chick).
evidence: Supported by photorefraction data shown in Figure 5C

claim: Application of +15 D lenses results in a myopic shift in refraction, compared to untreated eyes.
source: Application of –15 D lenses results in a hyperopic shift in the refraction of normal chick eyes, relative to untreated (no lens) eyes, whereas application of +15 D lenses results in a myopic shift in refraction, compared to untreated eyes. ***p<0.0001, ANOVA with Bonferroni correction for n=2 chicks in each group (five measurements/chick).
evidence: Supported by photorefraction data shown in Figure 5C
